subject: English
description: Direct to indirect — statements, questions, imperatives, tense backshift, time/place changes

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: She said, "I am writing a letter."

options.option_text: She said that she is writing a letter.
She said that she was writing a letter.
She told that she has been writing a letter.
She had said she will write a letter.

questions.explanation: Reporting verb in past tense (said) → tense backshifts: present continuous 'am writing' → past continuous 'was writing'. Pronoun 'I' (speaker) → 'she' (the original speaker, third person). Conjunction 'that' optional but standard. Use 'said' (intransitive) without an object; use 'told' only with an object: 'She told me that ...'. Standard backshifts: simple-present → simple-past; present-continuous → past-continuous; present-perfect → past-perfect; simple-past → past-perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said to the student, "Open your book."

options.option_text: The teacher said the student that he opens his book.
The teacher told the student to open his book.
The teacher said that the student opens the book.
The teacher ordered the student that he should open the book.

questions.explanation: IMPERATIVES (commands, requests, advice) → use the structure: 'reporting verb (told/ordered/requested/advised/asked) + object + to-infinitive'. 'Open your book' is an order → 'told the student to open his book'. Note: pronoun 'your' shifts to 'his' (referring to the student in 3rd person). For NEGATIVE imperatives: "Don't shout" → 'asked him NOT to shout'. Choice of reporting verb depends on tone — order (ordered/commanded), request (requested/asked), advice (advised), warning (warned).

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: He said, "Where do you live?"

options.option_text: He asked where do I live.
He asked where I lived.
He asked that where did I live.
He told where I am living.

questions.explanation: WH-questions in reported speech: (1) reporting verb 'said' → 'asked' / 'enquired'; (2) drop the auxiliary 'do/does/did' for the inverted-question form — use straight subject-verb word order; (3) keep the wh-word as a connector ('where', 'when', 'why', 'who', 'what', 'how'); (4) tense backshifts (do live → lived). Wrong patterns to avoid: 'asked where DO I live' (kept inversion — wrong); 'asked THAT where did I live' (used 'that' AND kept 'did' — both wrong). Yes/No questions use 'if'/'whether' instead: "Are you ready?" → 'asked if I was ready'.

questions.stem: Identify the correct indirect form: Ravi said, "I will meet you tomorrow."

options.option_text: Ravi said that he will meet me tomorrow.
Ravi said that he would meet me the next day.
Ravi told that he meets me tomorrow.
Ravi said that I would meet him the next day.

questions.explanation: Two transformations needed: (1) Modal backshift — 'will' → 'would'; (2) Time-expression shift — 'tomorrow' → 'the next day' / 'the following day'. Standard time/place shifts in reported speech: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day / the day before; last week → the previous week; next month → the following month; here → there; this → that; these → those; ago → before. Pronoun shifts: 'I' (Ravi) → 'he'; 'you' (the original listener, the reporter) → 'me'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: "Hurrah! We have won the match," he said.

options.option_text: He said that hurrah we won the match.
He exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
He told that we have won the match.
He shouted that they win the match.

questions.explanation: EXCLAMATORY sentences in reported speech: (1) reporting verb becomes 'exclaimed' / 'cried out' / 'shouted' + a phrase indicating the emotion ('with joy', 'with sorrow', 'in surprise', 'with regret'); (2) the interjection (Hurrah!, Alas!, Bravo!, Oh!) is dropped; (3) connector 'that'; (4) tense backshift — present-perfect 'have won' → past-perfect 'had won'; pronoun 'we' → 'they'. Common interjection mappings: Hurrah!/Bravo! → 'with joy/applause'; Alas! → 'with sorrow'; Oh! → 'in surprise'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said, "The earth revolves around the sun."

options.option_text: The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had revolved around the sun.
The teacher told that the earth was revolving around the sun.

questions.explanation: Important EXCEPTION to the tense-backshift rule: when the reported sentence is a UNIVERSAL TRUTH, scientific fact, geographical fact, habitual action that remains true, or a proverb — the present tense in the reported speech is RETAINED even if the reporting verb is in the past. Examples: 'He said that honesty IS the best policy' (proverb); 'She said that water BOILS at 100°C' (scientific fact); 'They said that the sun RISES in the east' (geographical fact). Tense backshift would suggest the fact stopped being true — which it didn't.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: She said to me, "Did you finish your homework?"

options.option_text: She asked me did I finish my homework.
She asked me if I had finished my homework.
She told me that I finished my homework.
She asked me whether did I finish my homework.

questions.explanation: YES/NO questions in reported speech: (1) reporting verb 'said' → 'asked' / 'enquired'; (2) connector 'if' OR 'whether' (NOT 'that'); (3) drop 'do/does/did' inversion → straight subject-verb order; (4) tense backshifts: simple-past 'did finish' → past-perfect 'had finished'. Pronouns: 'you' (the listener = me, the reporter) → 'I'; 'your' → 'my'. WRONG patterns: 'asked DID I finish' (kept inversion); 'asked WHETHER DID I finish' (kept 'did' AND used 'whether'); 'told' (told requires statements, not questions).

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: She said to him, "I can solve this problem easily."

options.option_text: She told him that I could solve this problem easily.
She told him that she could solve that problem easily.
She told him that she can solve that problem easily.
She said to him that she could solve that problem easily.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'said to' becomes 'told', the subject pronoun 'I' shifts to 'she' (the speaker), 'can' backhifts to 'could', and the demonstrative 'this' changes to 'that'. A is wrong because the pronoun stays as 'I' instead of shifting to 'she'. C is wrong because 'can' must shift to 'could' when the reporting verb is in the past tense. D is wrong because 'said to him' must be replaced by 'told him' in standard indirect speech.

questions.stem: Which is the correct indirect speech form of: He said, "I finished the report this morning."?

options.option_text: He said that he finished the report this morning still.
He said that he had finished the report that morning.
He said that he has finished the report that morning.
He said that he had finished the report this morning.

questions.explanation: B is correct: simple past 'finished' backhifts to past perfect 'had finished', and the time adverb 'this morning' shifts to 'that morning' in indirect speech. C is wrong because 'has finished' (present perfect) is not the correct backshift of simple past — that step is 'had finished'. D is wrong because the demonstrative time expression 'this morning' must change to 'that morning' when the reporting takes place at a later point.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: "Don't make noise in the library," the librarian said to the students.

options.option_text: The librarian asked the students that they must not make noise.
The librarian told the students not to make noise in the library.
The librarian warned the students for not making noise inside.
The librarian ordered students that they do not make noise inside.

questions.explanation: B is correct: negative imperatives in indirect speech follow the pattern 'told/asked + object + not to + base verb'. A is wrong because 'asked...that they must not' incorrectly uses a that-clause; reported imperatives require the infinitive construction. C is wrong because 'warned...for + gerund' is not the standard structure for reporting prohibitions. D is wrong because 'ordered...that they do not' is non-standard — reported commands use the to-infinitive, not a bare that-clause.

questions.stem: Identify the correct direct speech form of: She told her friend that she had missed the last bus that night.

options.option_text: She said to her friend, "I had missed the last bus that night."
She said to her friend, "I missed the last bus last night."
She said to her friend, "She missed the last bus last night."
She said to her friend, "I have missed the last bus last night."

questions.explanation: B is correct: reversing indirect to direct requires undoing the backshift (past perfect 'had missed' → simple past 'missed'), restoring the first-person pronoun ('she' the speaker → 'I'), and converting the time adverb ('that night' → 'last night'). A is wrong because it retains 'had missed' and 'that night', both of which are indirect-speech forms. C is wrong because the speaker refers to herself as 'I', not 'she', in direct speech. D is wrong because 'have missed' (present perfect) does not correspond to the indirect 'had missed'.

questions.stem: Which is the correct indirect form of: He said, "Let us plan the trip carefully"?

options.option_text: He said that they let plan the trip carefully together.
He suggested that they should plan the trip carefully.
He told that they must plan the trip very carefully.
He suggested them for planning the trip very carefully.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Let us' sentences express suggestions and are reported as 'suggested/proposed that + subject + should + base verb'. A is wrong because retaining 'let' with a bare infinitive in a that-clause is ungrammatical in indirect speech. C is wrong because 'told' requires an intervening object ('told them that…'), and 'must' converts a suggestion into an obligation, changing the meaning. D is wrong because 'suggested + object + for + gerund' is not the accepted structure for reporting suggestions.

questions.stem: Choose the CORRECT reported form of the optative sentence: "Would that I could fly like a bird!" he said.

options.option_text: He exclaimed that he wished to fly like a bird in sky.
He wished that he could fly like a bird at that moment.
He said that he would that he could fly like a bird then.
He wished that he might have flown like a bird freely.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Would that + subject + could/would' is an optative (wish) construction; its indirect form is 'wished that + subject + could + base verb'. The modal 'could' does not backshift further since it is already a past-form modal. A is wrong because 'exclaimed...wished to' drops the subordinate clause structure and loses the conditional nuance of the wish. C is wrong because 'would that' cannot be retained inside the reported clause — it must be replaced by 'wished that'. D is wrong because 'might have flown' (perfect modal) implies the wish has been missed, distorting the original meaning which simply expresses an unfulfilled desire.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: The inspector said to the witness, "What were you doing at 9 p.m. last night?"

options.option_text: The inspector asked the witness what he was doing at 9 p.m. last night.
The inspector asked the witness what he had been doing at 9 p.m. the previous night.
The inspector asked the witness that what had he been doing at 9 p.m. the night before.
The inspector asked the witness what he had done at 9 p.m. the previous night.

questions.explanation: B is correct: reporting a wh-question requires five simultaneous changes — (1) 'said to' → 'asked', (2) past continuous 'were you doing' → past perfect continuous 'had been doing', (3) 'you' → 'he', (4) 'last night' → 'the previous night', and (5) question word-order becomes statement word-order (no inversion). A is wrong because 'was doing' is only one tense step back (should be 'had been doing') and the time adverb 'last night' is unchanged. C is wrong because inserting 'that' before a wh-word is non-standard, and retaining the inversion 'had he been' incorrectly preserves question syntax inside the reported clause. D is wrong because 'had done' (simple past perfect) collapses the continuous aspect — the original 'were doing' denotes an ongoing action at a point in time, which must shift to 'had been doing', not 'had done'.
